title: LeBron James to 76ers: No Championship, Says NBA Exec
htmlContent:
LeBron James is heading to the Philadelphia 76ers. The NBA's all-time leading scorer announced the move on social media, calling it his "last decision" after a stretch in which he strongly considered retirement. The 41-year-old is reportedly signing a two-year, $8 million deal, a steep pay cut from the nearly $53 million he made last season with the Los Angeles Lakers.

But according to an NBA executive who spoke with LandonBuford.com, the move says less about James chasing a fifth title and more about where he actually stands in today's league, and where his influence may be headed next.

"I'm Using Common Sense"

The executive did not mince words when describing how the league office and rival front offices are reading the situation.

"I don't care what the media says. I don't care what Rich Paul says. I don't care what anybody says. I'm using common sense," the source told LandonBuford.com. "Cleveland didn't bring him back. The Lakers moved in a different direction. Miami didn't reunite with him. To me, that says everything about where LeBron James stands in the NBA today."

It's a blunt assessment of a player who is still, by nearly every measure, one of the most productive 41-year-olds the sport has ever seen. James averaged 20.9 points, 7.2 assists and 6.1 rebounds while shooting 51.5 percent from the field in 60 games last season, earning his 22nd consecutive All-Star selection. Still, the executive's point wasn't about James's talent — it was about how three organizations that know him best all chose to move forward without him.

One Last Run, Not One Last Title

In his own announcement, James framed the move in personal terms rather than championship terms.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time," he wrote, adding that he was "not going for money" or "family," but simply because he still wants to "sacrifice," "work" and "compete."

The 76ers haven't won an NBA championship since 1983 and haven't advanced past the second round of the Eastern Conference playoffs since 2001. On paper, pairing James withJoel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and newly acquired Jaylen Brown, the 2024 NBA Finals MVP, gives Philadelphia one of the more talented starting fives in the league. But the LandonBuford.com source isn't buying a storybook ending.

"At 41 years old, he's in Philadelphia for one last run, but I don't believe it's going to end with a championship. You can book it," the executive said, pointing to Embiid's injury history and the crowded championship field in the East as reasons for skepticism.

A City Where Sports and Politics Collide

What sets this executive's take apart is where the conversation goes next.

"Philadelphia is a city where sports and politics often intersect," the source said, noting that both James and Brown have long been willing to speak out on political and social issues. "LeBron James and Jaylen Brown have both been outspoken on political and social issues, and I wouldn't be surprised if they become influential voices in Pennsylvania beyond basketball."

James has a long track record of political engagement, from voting-rights initiatives to his "More Than a Vote" organization. Brown, meanwhile, has been active on labor and economic issues through his work with the National Basketball Players Association and his own advocacy initiatives. Landing two of the league's most politically vocal stars in the same locker room, in a state that regularly decides national elections, is not something the executive believes will go unnoticed.

Keeping an Eye on Josh Shapiro and 2028

The executive's opinion extends beyond the 2026–27 season and into presidential politics.

"If Governor Josh Shapiro runs for president in 2028, I think there will be plenty of discussion about whether prominent athletes like LeBron and Jaylen Brown choose to support his campaign or encourage voter participation," the source told LandonBuford.com. "That's my opinion, and it's something I'll be watching."

Shapiro, Pennsylvania's governor, has been mentioned frequently as a potential future Democratic presidential contender, and Pennsylvania's status as a perennial swing state means any high-profile endorsement or turnout push carries outsized weight. Whether James and Brown choose to lean into that role remains speculative, but the executive's framing places their arrival in Philadelphia inside a much bigger conversation than basketball alone.

What Happens On the Court — and Off It

For now, the basketball questions are the ones with a firm timeline. Training camp will reveal how quickly James, Embiid, Maxey and Brown can mesh, and Embiid's health will remain the swing factor in whether Philadelphia can genuinely contend in the East. The political questions, by contrast, won't have answers for years, if they ever fully materialize at all.

Still, as the executive put it in summing up the year ahead:

"The basketball season will determine what happens on the court. The political future will determine what happens off it."

For a franchise that hasn't tasted a title in over four decades, and a player writing what he's called his final chapter, both storylines are ones to watch.
excerpt: An NBA executive who spoke with LandonBuford.com says LeBron James's two-year, $8 million deal with the Philadelphia 76ers signals where he stands in today's league — and predicts the move will not end with a fifth championship ring.
